svg.aria-label: Diagram: Private Service Connect for Google APIs in Google Cloud, and how all four private access options compare; an endpoint replaces the public addresses of services such as storage.googleapis.com with an internal address in your own network, built on a global internal IP address reserved with the purpose flag set to PRIVATE_SERVICE_CONNECT; Service Directory region and namespace are shared by every Google API endpoint in a VPC network rather than set per endpoint, defaulting to us-central1 when no region is configured and to a system-generated namespace when none exists; and the comparison across the four options, where Private Service Connect endpoints serve Google Cloud resources or on-premises systems with or without external addresses and support all Google Cloud APIs and most other Google APIs, backends serve the same clients through a load balancer you own but support only selected locational and global APIs, Private Google Access serves only Google Cloud resources without external addresses and reaches the standard external addresses or the VIP domains through the default internet gateway, and Private Google Access for on-premises hosts serves on-premises hosts over a Cloud VPN tunnel or VLAN attachment with coverage depending on which VIP domain is chosen
svg.title: Private Service Connect for Google APIs: the widest of the four private access options
svg.text: Six posts, four ways to reach a Google API privately. This is the one that fits every client.
“Instead of sending API requests to the publicly available IP addresses … send them to the
internal IP address of an endpoint.”
The address is GLOBAL, INTERNAL, and purpose-tagged
gcloud compute addresses create NAME --global --purpose=PRIVATE_SERVICE_CONNECT
--addresses=ENDPOINT_IP --network=NETWORK_NAME
Global, not regional — one address serves the network. The purpose flag is what makes it an
endpoint address rather than an ordinary reservation.
Service Directory is set PER NETWORK, not per endpoint
ALL endpoints for Google APIs in a VPC network share the SAME Service Directory REGION, and
the SAME NAMESPACE. The first endpoint sets them; the rest inherit.
Defaults worth knowing: no region configured → us-central1. No namespace configured → a
system-generated one is assigned.
The four options, by who can use them and what they reach
1. PSC ENDPOINTS for Google APIs — the widest
CLIENTS: Google Cloud resources OR on-premises systems, WITH OR WITHOUT external IPs
PATH: to an endpoint in your VPC network, which forwards to Google APIs
REACHES: ALL Google Cloud APIs and most other Google APIs and services
No external-IP precondition, no VIP, no on-premises special case.
2. PSC BACKENDS for Google APIs — same clients, narrower reach
CLIENTS: the same — Google Cloud resources or on-premises, with or without external IPs
PATH: to a LOAD BALANCER in your VPC network, which forwards to Google APIs
REACHES: only SELECTED locational and global Google APIs. Your load balancer costs you coverage.
3. PRIVATE GOOGLE ACCESS — narrowest client set
CLIENTS: Google Cloud resources WITHOUT external IP addresses. That is the whole precondition.
PATH: to the standard external addresses, or the VIP domains, through the DEFAULT INTERNET
GATEWAY — #90’s paradox, restated here in one line.
REACHES: most Google APIs and services.
4. PRIVATE GOOGLE ACCESS FOR ON-PREMISES HOSTS
CLIENTS: on-premises hosts, with or without external IP addresses
PATH: over a Cloud VPN tunnel or VLAN attachment, using one of the VIP domains
REACHES: depends entirely on WHICH VIP domain you chose — #92’s decision, still binding.
Reading the table as a decision
Only one option has no client precondition and the widest API coverage. The other three each
trade something away: a load balancer narrows coverage, no external IP is a hard gate, and the
on-premises route inherits whichever VIP you committed to three posts ago.
